name: economy
title: Economy
scope: Intro economics for gross domestic product, inflation as a rising price level, opportunity cost, and the direction of supply and demand.
method: Say whether you need a definition, an identity, or the direction of a change.
For output, expand GDP into consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports.
Treat inflation as a sustained rise in the general price level, using a price index rather than one good.
State opportunity cost as the single next-best alternative given up by a choice.
For supply and demand, name which curve shifts and hold the other curve fixed.
Report how equilibrium price and quantity move, and do not invent a numerical price.
Call the result a textbook relation, not advice about what anyone should do.

formulas.name: Expenditure GDP
formulas.use: Gross domestic product on the expenditure side adds consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports.

formulas.name: Net exports
formulas.use: Net exports equal exports minus imports and are the NX term in GDP.

formulas.name: Inflation rate
formulas.use: The inflation rate is the fractional rise in a general price index over one period.

formulas.name: Opportunity cost
formulas.expr: cost = value of the next best alternative given up
formulas.use: A choice's opportunity cost is the single best thing not chosen, not the sum of every rejected option.

checks: A GDP sum is incomplete until C, I, G, and NX are all accounted for.
One product costing more is not, by itself, inflation of the general price level.
Higher demand with supply fixed raises equilibrium price and quantity; higher supply with demand fixed lowers equilibrium price and raises quantity.
Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative forgone, not every other option added together.
limits: This is not investment advice and not a forecast.
Identities and curve directions do not say what a person, firm, or government should do.
The card has no live statistics; a measured GDP or inflation figure needs a named data source.
